speechtext:
On the 9th of June the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) asked the following question which will be found in Hansard of that date:
Mr. J. E. Armstrong (East Lambton) :	I
should like to ask the Government whether it is true that the Imperial Government has appointed an Imperial Board of Investigation for the purpose of inquiring into trade relations between different parts of the British Empire; whether Sir George Perley has been appointed a member of that board, and when the findings of the board, if such has been appointed, may be expected. I should also like to know whether the

board will Inquire into trade or tariff agreements, and into the tolls or arrangements entered into between the different shipping companies within the Empire?
In answer to this question, I would say that:
1.	No such Board has yet been constituted; but the Government have under consideration certain proposals submitted by His Majesty's Government for the constitution of an Imperial Investigation Board to be set up by the Governments of the Empire in pursuance of Resolutions XI and XIV of the Imperial War Conference, 1918. It is proposed that the Board shall have power to inquire into complaints with regard to ocean freights, facilities and conditions in the inter-imperial trade and into similar questions referred to them by the various governments; to survey the facilities for maritime transport within the Empire and to make recommendations for the co-ordination and improvement of such facilities.
2.	Such a board not having been finally constituted, no definite ' appointment has yet been made.
3.	Answered by paragraph 1.
4.	Since the receipt of the proposals mentioned in paragraph 1 a proposal has been put forward to the Imperial Government by the Prime Minister of Canada on behalf of the Government of Canada that full power as to the control of ocean rates and the disposition of the shipping of the British Empire be conferred by concurrent legislation upon a temporary commission representative of the United Kingdom and the Dominions; and that a committee representative of the United Kingdom and the Dominions shall be immediately set up for the purpose of framing a permanent scheme for the same purpose and for the general development of ocean transportation within the Empire. The Prime Minister has further suggested that this proposal be considered in connection with that described in paragraph 1 and has declared that the Government of Canada will be glad to join in the discussion as soon as the Government of the United Kingdom is prepared to consider the matter.

The House resumed the debate on the motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance), that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means (resumed from Tuesday, June 10).
Hon. THOMAS ALEXANDER CRERAR
(late Minister of Agriculture):	Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact of my severing

my connection with the Government, I think it is only proper on this occasion that I should refer briefly to the circumstances wfhich led to my joining the ministry in October, 1917, as well as to those which led to my withdrawal from it. In the summer of 1917 it was quite cleaa- that a very serious and difficult situation faced the Canadian people. There had been in Western Canada, and particularly in the case of the organized body of public opinion in that part of the Dominion with which I had been identified, a strong desire that some sort of national or union government should be formed in order that Canada might more effectively, or as effectively as possible, contribute her share to the winning of the struggle that was being fought out on the fields of Europe. Consequently, when the Prime Minister invited me to join his Government, in a sense representing that body of organized public opinion to which I have referred, I considered it my duty to do so.
I took that step at that time entirely from a sense of duty, and I have to say that under similar circumstances I would take the same step again.
Hear, hear.

When I joined the
Government I made it perfectly clear that I had not surrendered or given up any of the principles that I believed in and as to which I had endeavoured, in my small way, to educate this country prior to that event. However, there was one outstanding issue at that time, and everything else was overshadowed by the importance of that issue. But now, Sir, the war in over, the armistice was signed over seven months ago, and we are shortly, we hope, to witness a peace among the nations of the earth that will be lasting in its character and will forever in the future prevent a repetition of the catastrophe that has overwhelmed the world in the last four and a half years. Such being the case, when it came to a consideration of what the fiscal policy of this country should be in the future, I found myself in sharp issue with the Government, and holding the views that I did, and representing in the Cabinet, in a measure, the opinion of the farmers of Canada- although I quite recognized that I was not a representative there of any special class, I want to make that clear-and knowing the opinion of the farmers of Western Canada on the fiscal question, and believing absolutely in it myself, there was I felt only one course for me to follow when
I found myself at issue with my colleagues and that was to tender my resignation to the Prime Minister, which I did.
Hear, hear.

Having said so much, Mr. Speaker, I shall endeavour to sketch briefly before the House the reasons that induced.me to take the step that I did. The war is over, and we are now facing the settlement of the accounts that have arisen by reason of that war. The one fact to my mind that stands out like a beacon light in the Budget proposals presented to the House the other day by the Finance Minister is, that the national debt of Canada at the end of the present fiscal year will be $1,950,000,000, and that Canada will require to raise annually a revenue of at least $300,000,000. Moreover, if we examine the circumstances of the case, we 6hall find, I think,-that even that sum will scarcely suffice to meet our requirements. The Finance Minister has estimated that this year we will require $102,000,000 for interest on our public debt, and he further estimates that at the end of the fiscal year the obligation in that respect will have grown to $115,000,000. For pensions, we have to provide $30,000,000, and I quite expect that before the aftermath of the war in respect of the allotment of pensions is cleaned up, that our pension bill will probably run to $35,000,000 a year. In addition we have, as the result of shall I say mistaken policies in the past, and I do not wish to attribute blame anywhere in that regard, to provide for several years to come probably $10,000,000 a year to meet the deficits on our national railways. In other words, Mr. Speaker, we will be obliged to produce from the revenues of Canada at least $150,000,000 a year more than was required in pre-war days. Canada we must bear in mind is an expensive country to govern. The boundless distances of our country, our scattered population, and the necessity of carrying on needed and necessary public works in the various portions of the Dominion mean this: that for years to come our expenditures in a capital way upon river and harbour improvements, and the various other public necessities, will run into very considerable figures. So I think I am within the mark when I state that the public revenue of Canada will require to be at least $300,000,000 a year for a good many years to come, and even that makes no provision for a sinking fund to retire our debt as it matures. Now, how is this bur-

den to be met? That is the paramount question in my judgment before the Canadian people to-day. The amount of money that a country raises for its public needs is of importance, but the manner in which that money is raised is of vastly greater importance, and here is where I take issue with the present proposals of the Finance Minister.	.
No question has so agitated civilized nations-in fact, I think I am well within the mark when I say that no question has been so influential in bringing about reforms in governmental administration down through the ages than that as to the method by which the taxes of a country are levied. It is the paramount question for the people, because, if your tax burden is inequitably distributed, you have injustice and discontent, and, as has been proved by past history, you sometimes have had produced thereby the seeds of revolution itself.
Now, we propose, under the present Budget, to raise our taxes mainly by the imposition of customs and excise duties. Before I discuss that, however, let me say this: In my opinion the present Budget is a protectionist Budget. I think there is no disguising that fact. In 1915 special customs taxes were imposed for the purpose of raising revenue. There is no need now for my discussing the merits or demerits of that action; but by that Act $45,000,000 of additional taxes were levied on the Canadian people last year by way of customs taxation. The proposals that have been placed before the House contain certain provisions that mean a reduction of that taxation to the extent of $17,000,000 a year, and if the present values of imported goods hold we shall collect this year under that arrangement $28,000,000. Just here I offer my first criticism. By what virtue of justice or equity is the 7} per cent removed from certain articles and left on others? That, to my mind, can find no justification. There have been reductions beyond the 7} per cent, which has been taken off a limited number of articles. The 7} per cent that was imposed in 1915 has been removed from all agricultural implements, and we have further concessions in the matter of agricultural implements to the extent of 5 per cent on farm wagons, hay-loaders and certain other implements; a reduction from 27} per cent to 15 per cent on cultivators, seed-drills, etc., that is, including the elimination of the 7} per cent, and a reduction from 27} per cent to 17} per cent on ploughs, engines and tractors.
[Mr. Crerar.j
But there is another aspect of this matter that is open to criticism. The removal of the duty of 5 per cent, in addition to the removal of the 7} per cent on the items that I have specified, does not mean any lessened protection to the manufacturer in Canada who is making those goods, because an arrangement has been made with the Canadian railways for a reduction in freights from manufacturing points, chiefly in Ontario, to Western Canada, in order to offset what is lost by the withdrawal of the 5 per cent. On the other hand, the railways are to have the benefit of the abolition of the 7} per cent duty on bituminous coal coming into Canada. Here I have another criticism to offer. Why is the discrimination made in favour of the farmer in Western Canada, as against, say, the farmer in the Maritime Provinces? In my judgment, the proposal is unsound in that respect.	It is quite clear,
at any rate to me, why that provision has- been made. Western Canada- at any rate, the agricultural portion of it -has stated in unmistakable terms its opinion on the matter of customs duties on agricultural implements, and this concession in the Budget is merely a concession to attempt to satisfy opinion in Western Canada and to do it in such a way that the manufacturers do not suffer, and the users of implements throughout the rest of Canada are discriminated against. That, Mr. Speaker, is not a sound proposal; it is not a logical proposal; it is introducing into the shaping of our fiscal policy principles which are unsound, which are not in the best interests of Canada, and which are calculated to bring about dissension and difficulty. It is a poor policy to mix up freight rates with tariffs.
I should like to examine for a few moments the effect of the policy of protection upon the national development of the Dominion. If we are to overcome the tremendous burden of debt that is upon us- and I do not think there will be any disposition on the part of the Canadian people to shirk that duty-and if we are to obtain the enormous revenues that we shall annually require to carry on the business of the country, how best can we do it? After all, that is the practical question which faces the House and the country to-day.
Now, Canada is a country of great natural wealth. We have our agriculture, our minerals, our fisheries, and our splendid timber resources; and the problem before this House to-day is, how best can these resources be soundly and wisely developed? I have never been able to see any virtue

in the principle of protection. Theoretically, if the principle of protection is sound, why not build your tariff wall so high that no goods can come in? But if you build your tariff wall so high that no goods can come in, then no goods go out, because goods are bought with goods. If we export goods from Canada, whether agricultural products, manufactured goods, or whatever they may be, those exports must be paid for by imports. If the protectionist theory is sound, it should be carried to the extent,
I believe, suggested by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) when he was discussing this matter in the House on a previous occasion-the building of a tariff wall so high around Canada that all goods would be kept out. Well, that does not appeal to me as a very sensible proposition.
But if we are going to develop our resources, how best can we do it? Shall we do it most effectively and efficiently by imposing burdens of taxation upon the machinery and the equipment necessary to this development and to this production? Canada is one of the finest agricultural countries in the world; she has a wonderful future, agriculturally, if we are but wise in our policies. We are aiming to place returned soldiers on the land; we are providing in our financial proposals of this year $25,000,000 for that purpose. We are hoping to secure from Great Britain immigrants who will go upon the land. There is a consensus of opinion that our immigration in the future should be of a class of people who will go upon the land and develop our agricultural possibilities; we already have enough people in the cities.
But when we place a returned soldier upon	the land,	we have to start	himout with equipment. It is useless to put	him down	on a	homestead	andsay:	Now, here	you	are. He cannotgrow	grain nor	raise	cattle with	his
hands alone. He requires equipment, agricultural machinery, horses and harness to put on those horses. But when we ask him to do that work, we immediately say to him, on the other hand: You must, however, In the purchase of the equipment that goes into the production of the stuff you hope to produce from your farm, pay to the State, twenty per cent of the value of the equipment you get. What does that mean? If a returned soldier or an immigrant has $2,000 and wishes to go on to the land to develop it, he first buys his equipment. If he could buy it tax free, so far as customs duties are concerned, he could buy it for $1,600, and he would have $400 as a working
capital to start upon, to carry on his operations.
How could he be free from taxation? Would he not have to pay taxes somehow?

I was speaking about customs taxes, and I think if my hon. friend reflects a moment, he will get my point.
The same thing is true in respect to the development of our mineral, lumbering and fishery resources. It is sound policy to provide as cheaply as possible the equipment required by the people who are going to dig the wealth out of the earth where, after all, it must come from. Therefore, any fiscal policy that imposes handicaps on that, that throws disabilities around it, retards, in my judgment, just to that extent, the development of the country. But what have been the results in agriculture in Ontario-and I would direct attention to that, because Ontario is probably the greatest manufacturing province in the Dominion? It is a fact that nobody can deny that agriculture has gone back in Ontario since the introduction of the National Policy in 1879. Prior to that time the rural population outnumbered in great degree the city population, but there has been a steady decline in the rural population of Ontario. It may be argued, and, I recognize, with some force, that that is not due to the tariff; that a number of Ontario farmers have moved to Western Canada, and that perhaps a number have moved to the United States.

My hon. friend argues that Ontario has gone back agriculturally because its rural population is less now than it was some years ago. Then it must be true that the West has gtme ahead because its rural population is greater now than it was some years ago. Does the hon. member accept that position?

If my hon. friend will be patient for a moment, I think I can elaborate my argument so that his question would have been unnecessary. I repeat again that agriculture has been going backward in Ontario instead of forward, and the evidence of that lies in this, that the volume of agricultural products produced in old Ontario under normal conditions-I am not speaking of the higher values that appertain as a result of war conditions-are less to-day than they were thirty years ago. Furthermore-and the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) knows it-he can travel
3332 '

through Ontario as I have travelled through it, and he will find not hundreds but thousands of abandoned farms in that province.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us where those abandoned farms are?
Let the canners keep q.uiet.
Can your question.

Within the last two years I saw myself in a twelve-mile drive in the county of Huron, one of the best counties of Ontario, six vacant farms, and I have no reason to doubt the statement I have made. With the decrease in the rural population of Ontario, there has been an increase in the city population. If hon. members will study the municipal statistics of Ontario, recently published, they. will find that the decrease in the township population of Ontario for the years 1916 and 1917 was
36,000,	and the increase in the city population of that province during the same period was practically the same. The reason of that is that the farmers of Ontario-I am speaking of the average case-have found it difficult and are to-day finding it difficult to make more than both ends meet. I have here a statement published by the department of farm management connected with the Ontario Agricultural College at Guelph, giving a survey of a large number of farms in Oxford county which, next to Huron county, is probably the banner county of Ontario from an agricultural point of view. It is a great dairying county. This is the conclusion reached by the department of farm management:
It is plain, therefore, from the above figures that to give the average dairyman of Oxford a fair return for his labour', 7 per cent interest on his investment, and 2 per cent additional on his capital for a reserve fund and a reasonable profit that he should have received at least an average of $2.49 per hundred pounds for his milk during the year ending February 28, 1918.
What is the average price he received? According to the same report, it is $2.20 per hundred pounds. 'J'hat is the reason why agriculture is backward in Ontario. How can it be set up? You must, in my judgment, cheapen the processes of production. If you place a handicap on production, if the equipment-I do not care what it is called-that enters into that production has the price of it enhanced, the result is inevitable that the margin of profit to the farmer shrinks, and as is the case in this instance, gets practically to the vanishing point.

As regards the western farmers, in those localities and districts where farmers secured their land years ago at reasonable prices and where they have been favoured with good crops, they have done very well, but I am certain that if you take the average of the farmers of Western Canada, if you take into consideration the vicissitudes they have suffered from in crop failures of one kind or another, the average return is not very great. We have spoken about an immigration policy, and we need immigration into this country. We must increase our population, but the best immigration agent in Canada is the contented citizen. If you have a country in which the average ordinary man can make a living and provide against want in his old age, you have a good country to live in, and that fact will be made known throughout the world, and will attract people to your shores.
I come to another aspect of the question, namely: Do our implement manufacturers really require the protection which they enjoy? On looking up the statistics I find that in 1914 exports of agricultural implements from Canada amounted to $7,900,000; in 1915, $3,650,000; in 1916, $3,850,000, and in 1917, $4,040,000. You will note that there has been a decline in the last three years, but that I attribute to the fact that the energies of our manufacturing plants were directed into other channels. In other words, there was scarcely a foundry or factory in Canada that was not pressed into the urgent and imperative need of manufacturing war supplies. But the year 1914 is a fair year to take, and I ask this question: If our agricultural implement manufacturers can export $7,900,000 of goods in one year into the markets of the world, where they have to compete with every one else who is making agricultural implements, why cannot they compete at home? That is the question. Why should it be necessary to impose taxes to the extent of 15, 20, 26 or 30 per cent on agricultural implements necessary to the development of this country when our implement manufacturers in this country have been able so to establish their business-and I am proud of it, great credit is due them-that they can compete in the markets of the world to the extent of almost $8,000,000 a year.
There is another item. Over twenty years ago one lone agricultural implement was placed on the free list in Canada. That was cream separators. What has been the result, to the cream separator industry in this country? Did it languish and die because protection was withdrawn from it? It did

not. On the contrary, I am glad to say that it has gone ahead, and to-day we have eleven plants in Canada manufacturing cream separators, and three plants manufacturing cream separators exclusively, and not only are our manufacturers selling their cream separators in Canada in competition with separators manufactured in other parts of the world, but they are selling cream separators in the United States in competition with cream separators manufactured in that country. What enters into the manufacture of a cream separator? Precisely the same elements as enter into the manufacture of any other agricultural implement. In fact, if anything it is more difficult to manufacture a cream separator because, being a more finely adjusted machine, its manufacture requires much more skill and ingenuity than for instance a wagon or a seed drill.
There is another industry in Canada that has been carrying on without the protection of the tariff, and that is the bijider twine industry. I find, according to the Canada Year Book, that in the year 1916 Canadian made binder twine was exported from Canada to the extent of 17,000,000 pounds, to compete with twine manufactured elsewhere in the world. Let me say again, I am proud of the fact, because it shows what our Canadian manufacturers standing on their own resources can do. I am satisfied that our manufacturers with the application of the same methods could obtain the same results in any line of agricultural implements.
There is one other way in which the tariff bears very heavily upon the people at the present time, and that is in the cost of living. It was perhaps inevitable that serious unrest would develop as a result of the cataclysm through which the world has been passing during the last four or five years. There is no patriotic Canadian who loves his country who does not regret the fact that there is such unrest in Canada to-day practically from one end of the country to the other, for I doubt if there is a city of any magnitude in this country where there is not at the present time labour disturbance of some kind or another. Whenever the question is raised, the invariable answer is that the problem to be solved' is the high cost of living- that there, the remedy lies. I submit that one of the most effective means of striking at the high cost of living in Canada to-day is through the customs tariff. What does the ordinary man in Canada require- and, after alii, we must bear in mind that
the great majority of Canadians are humble citizens doing their work in humble walks of life-they require food, clothing, shelter. These are absolute necessities to any person living in Canada. When the workingman in Canada buys much of the food that is necessary for his sustenance, its cost is made greater by the fact that it. is taxed anywhere from 20 to 25 per cent when it enters Canada, and the same is true of his clothing and boots and shoes. Why cannot we do in Canada what they have done in the United States, make boots and shoes free to the people? I have not had an opportunity of reading yesterday's Hansard, but I notice in the press this morning that the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Scott) stated in the House yesterday that there was very little difference between prices of shoes in the United States and Canada. If that is true, there is absolutely no need of a protective tariff to the extent of 30 per cent to keep American shoes out of Canada, but I am afraid that if the hon. member will search his sources of information a little more closely he will find that the facts do not substantiate entirely what he has stated.
We knew better.

I was recently talking to a man who was pricing shoes and clothing in the United States in comparison with Canadian prices, and in every case he found that prices were higher in Canada, practically to the extent of the duty imposed. That is inevitable. Why is the duty im' posed if it is not to keep other goods out, because they are cheaper? Consequently, if we are going to strike at the high cost of living we can do it effectively in this way, and I know of no other way at present in which it can be done.
We have a commission travelling over Canada-and it was a laudable effort on the part of the Government-endeavouring to ascertain, and if possible harmonize, the conflicting views of employers and employees in Canadian industry. We have today a committee of this House investigating the high cost of living. It is one of the paramount questions before the Canadian people to-day, and it does seem to me that one effective way to solve the problem is the one I have suggested.
For the year 1913, the family budget for five persons amounted to $1,051.74. That budget to-day amounts to $1,668.91, or an increase of almost 60 per cent. I have also another illustration which I desire to place before the House. The information

I am about to give was furnished by a clothing dealer in the city of Winnipeg, and I have every assurance that it is entirely reliable. In 1914 the invoice price of a suit of clothes from the Old Country was, say, $10. The duty added would be $3, and after calculating the profits that would go to the various people handling the clothes, the value of the suit at the time it was purchased by the wearer amounted to $22.36. Now, at that time, without a duty of 30 per cent which was levied, the suit would cost $17.51. But what is the situation in 1919? The suit of clothes has gone up in value to the manufacturer to $25, and the duty added is $8.75-that is, up to the recent change in the new financial proposals-with a result that when you add the various profits the suit of clothes costs the wearer $58.21. If it had come duty free the person purchasing it would get it now for $43.12. These are facts, and I think that it is beyond any question of doubt that so far as clothing is concerned the customs tariff does add to the price and thereby increase the cost of living.

Would the hon.
gentleman tell us how many bushels of wheat it would take to buy that suit of clothes?

With wheat at 80
cents a bushel in 1914 the farmer could purchase this suit of clothes with 28 bushels. In 1919, with the increased cost he requires to get $2 a bushel for 29 bushels of wheat to buy the same suit. Furthermore, a wage earner could get
4 p.m. a similar suit of clothes for nine days' work at $2.50 per day in 1914; now, he has to work nine days at $6.50 a day to buy it.
In this connection I should like to quote a newspaper item which I am confident is quite correct from the manner in which it is given. It deals with profits made by the Dominion Textile Company last year and during the past few years. Let me read it:
Manufacturing profits for the year recently ended were $3,434,752, against $1,803,371 in 1.917-18, an increase of $1,561,381, or in excess of 83 per cent, and substantially more than double those of the previous year. There is one other suggestion and perhaps I may be regarded as stating the most radical thing that I have proposed in my discussion of this subject. That is the suggestion that a direct tax should be imposed on the unimproved value of land including all natural resources. I want to make clear the distinction in this regard. It does not mean a land tax in the ordinary sense of the word. It means a tax on the value of land. This principle has been applied in the Western Provinces. Now the proposal underlying this is, that land shall be taxed-not that land alone, but all land -on its unimproved value. Hon. JAMES ALEXANDER CALDER
(Minister of Immigration and Colonization) : Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks, I desire to congratulate the Finance Minister upon the splendid address which he delivered to the House in presenting his Budget proposals. I have listened to some Budget speeches in this House and in the old Commons chamber, and I have read a good many, and I cannot recall a single one in which the financial position of the country was set forth so simply, so plainly, and so clearly, as it was last Thursday afternoon. I consider that the Budget which was then presented was an honest Budget- honest in that there was no attempt at concealment. I am sure that all the members of this House have been anxious to learn the truth, and the whole truth, as regards the financial position of Canada at the present time. I think every hon. gentleman will agree with me that we have got that desideratum and more than that, we are indebted to the Finance Minister, regardless of whether we agree with his proposals or not, for the very great care and the skill with which he marshalled his facts and presented them to the House.
In addressing the House at this time it is not my intention to speak at length; the occasion does not demand it. I wish to state simply that I intend to support the Budget proposals which have been submitted to the House, and I shall explain as clearly and as definitely as I can why I intend to do so. To attain that end, I do not think that a very elaborate arguement is necessary.
We have listened to an able and very interesting address from my former colleague, the member for Marquette (Hon. T. A. Crerar) with regard to the Budget proposals. He has set forth his views clearly, sincerely, *and honestly. I am sure that no member of the House will quarrel with him in the view that he takes; least of all should I quarrel with him. Every member of this House is the keeper of his own conscience. We must all make up our minds as to what is right or vrhat is wrong on an occasion of this kind; each must determine his own



course and be 'held responsible for the course which he takes. The member for Marquette, after deliberate consideration and for the reasons which he has stated, has come to the conclusion that he cannot support the Budget.
Having regard to the conditions existing in Canada, to the problems that are before us, and to all the circumstances, I have, after very full consideration, come to the conclusion that no other course is open to me at the present time than to support the Budget proposals of the Finance Minister. More than that, I am convinced that I can do so without sacrificing any principles that I hold, without sacrificing my views on the tariff. Some hon. gentlemen opposite smile. I say that I can do it without sacrificing my principles or my views on the tariff and without prejudicing the interests of the province from which I come or of the constituents whom I represent.
In September or October, 1917, with the member for Marquette and others, I attended a series of conferences called for the purpose of deciding whether we should have in this country, at least for the time being, a National or Union Government. It is not necessary for me to review the circumstances; all members of the House are well acquainted with them. But at that time decisions had to foe reached that were bound to have far-reaching consequences, personal, political, and otherwise. No one who attended those conferences approached the problem confronting us with greater earnestness and greater seriousness than the member for Marquette, whose decision, I think I can safely say, was very largely instrumental in bringing about the result finally reached. The Government was formed in due course, and for the last eighteen months we have been carrying on as best we could. I intimated to the House early in the session that we had made mistakes.
Hear, hear.
Quite right. A Government that would not make mistakes in times like these is not worthy of the name-
You mean, "blunders."
Oh, oh.

Well, probably some
of my hon. friends on the other side do not know it, but nevertheless the statement I make is true. When the Government was constituted, it was composed of Liberals and Conservatives, and the members compromising the Government held strongly divergent views on the tariff question. There was no misunderstanding as to that when the Government was formed, and there is no misunderstanding now. We recognized at that time that those differences existed, and" we decided to lay aside our difference for the time being. We all realized that when the war was over, when peace was concluded and our soldiers were home, other questions would arise, and difficulties would stare us in the face, and we accepted the position realizing just what it was.
What is true of members of the Government is equally true of members of the House on both sides. The members of this House were not elected because of their tariff leanings. I do not wish to be personal, but let me take one or two illustrations. Let me take the hon. member who represents the constituency of Macdonald (Mr. Henders), who is and has been for a number of years, president of the Grain Growers' Association of Manitoba, a man highly respected by every person in that province and outside of it as well. Would any person say that when he was elected by the large majority he got it was because of the tariff issue? The hon. member for Macdonald was supported by all sections of the people in his constituency regardless of any opinions he held on the tariff, because, I say again, the tariff was not an issue when he was elected as a member of this House. Coming to my own province, let me take the hon. gentleman who comes from my home city, Regina (Mr. Cowan), a constituency that is normally Liberal. For the last fifteen or twenty years no Conservative has been elected in that constituency either to the provincial legislature or to this House. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan) secured the nomination, won the election, and in Regina alone he had a majority of over 4,000 votes. Will any person say that the people of that constituency were at that time thinking of the tariff or of a general revision of the tariff? They were not. At that time the people were thinking of and voting on the issue that was before the country.
They had the War-time Elections Act.

Yes, we had the Wartime Elections Act, but let me tell my hon. friend that a dozen War-time Elections Acts in Regina would never have given my hon. friend from that city 4,000 of a majority in a part of a constituency that had been Liberal for the last twenty years. Let me take my own case. Part of the constituency which I represent consists of Moosejaw, a city of some 25,000 people a city that has been Conservative in its leanings for the last fifteen or twenty years. Ever since the province was established, we have had a Conservative member from Moosejaw and when that city gave me a majority of 2,000 votes, it did not do so on the tariff question. The point I desire to make is this: that under the circumstances conneoted with the creation of the Government and under the conditions

under which the last elections were held, it is not strange if in this House we have differences of opinion and do not all see eye to eye on the tariff question.
The same is true to some extent of the Opposition. We have all been witnesses of the fact that in their ranks they are not a unit; they are not all free traders. If I am not mistaken, there are amongst them at least some moderate protectionists, and I think if I could peer into the minds of, shall I say, a good many, I would find among them some high protectionists.
Mighty few.

One need not be
surprised at that because hon. gentlemen opposite when they were elected, were not elected on the tariff question; they were elected, to oppose Union Government; they were elected to oppose the enforcement of the Military Service Act. Their constituents were not thinking of tariff questions when they elected hon. gentlemen opposite to this House. Therefore, it is not surprising if hon. gentlemen opposite are not a unit on this tariff question.
As a consequence of the general situation which I have described as regards both the supporters of the Government and the Opposition, we are all more or less apparently in an embarrassing position. But, to my mind it is more apparent than real, because, after all, the question which this House must decide at this juncture in the history of Canada in connection with the tariff question which has arisen, is whether or not the Government as now constituted in this country should be allowed to carry on.
The question which every member of this House must consider is whether or not the time has arrived when the existing Administration should make way for some other Administration^ That is the real question before the House at this moment. The tariff proposals that have been brought down are merely of a tentative or temporary character, and any hon. member who supports those proposals does not necessarily approve the principle or the details of any permanent tariff policy for this country. As a member of the Government I take the ground that in supporting these proposals I am not committing myself to principles at all.
In his Budget speech the Minister of Finance made this statement, and I would ask every hon. member to follow it closely to see just what it means:
It is my hope that within a year, conditions will have become so stabilized as to permit of

a general revision of the tariff, which is long, but, owing to the war, unavoidably overdue. Preceding such revision there should be a thorough inquiry conducted by the Minister of Finance and two or more of his colleagues representing the different geographical sections of Canada. Such inquiry should afford all interests, agricultural, industrial, fishing, lumbering, mining, commercial, and financial, producers and consumers alike, an opportunity of expressing their views and opinions and urging their particular needs and requirements. The result of such inquiry should he a body of information which will enable the Government to effect a general revision of the tariff fair to all parts of the community, and effectually promoting the national welfare of Canada. This inquiry should proceed with its work just as soon as conditions are sufficiently stabilized to permit. My own view is that it might well be commenced about autumn of this year.
Personally I am in accord with the views expressed in that statement.
The time has arrived, I believe, when t thorough study should be made of Canada's economic situation in order that we may have a general revision of the tariff. The existing tariff, in my judgment, has outlived its usefulness. It was made for a period some ten or twelve years ago, and it is chock-full of all sorts of anomalies which should be straightened out. A thorough investigation and inquiry, as forecasted by the Minister of Finance, should be made with a view to having a general revision of the tariff. When that time arrives it seems to me that it will be the duty of the Prime Minister to consult his colleagues as to the principles that should underlie the revision of the tariff. It is quite conceivable that his colleagues will not all agree and that there may be changes in the personnel of the Cabinet. But that time is not yet. These proposals now before us are merely of a temporary character. The time must come when, if we are to have a general revision of the tariff, there .must !be a clear and definite understanding as to the principles which should underlie that revision. Then it will be the duty and the right of every minister of the Crown who happens to be in the Government at that time to decide upon his course of actiou. When the revision of the tariff is before the House for approval, when we are dealing with the matter in a broad and general way, it will be the duty and the privilege of every member of this House to take such course of action as he deems necessary.
If I desired to do the popular thing at the present time, I would follow the example of my former colleague (Mr. Crerar). I say that if I desired to do the popular thing, if I wished to make a hero of my-

self, the road is quite clear; it would be a very easy road to take. If I wished to have my name acclaimed in every part of Western Canada, and in every corner of my own province, it would not take very long to attain that. But I have not taken that course, and I do not intend to. I do not intend to do so, because I do not believe it is right to do so.
As I have stated before in this House, many of my friends have implored me to leave the Government long ere this, and they have prophesied what is going to happen to me. T have had threats, very many of them, but I have turned a deaf ear to them all, and I have done so because I believe that during the past year and a half I have steered the only course that I could properly and conscientiously steer. When I joined the Government in 1917 I did so for a very definite and specific reason. I did so because I believed the proposals that were put forward at that time set out the only policy that would enable Canada to see this war through, so far as our part in it was concerned. I do not purpose to allow any temporary changes in the tariff to divert me from my duty in that respect as I see it.

Suppose the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) resigned, and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell), and the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Maclean), and myself and others should resign.
Oh, oh.

Hear, hear.

Well, I will ask in all
seriousness: is that the will of Parliament, and is it the wish of the people of this country?
Yes.
No.

Is that the wish of the
members of this House who are inclined to .criticise and vote against the Budget proposals? I think I am putting the situation squarely and fairly before the House. As I see the situation in Canada and as I see it right in this House, I am impelled to say that the people of Canada to-day are demanding sacrifices just as much as they did in the days of the war. They are demanding sacrifice on the part of public men in this country-sacrifice, not of principle but of self-and I am afraid that there are some people who are thinking rather of self at this time than of the public interest. So far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I would have been perfectly satisfied if the tariff had not been touched at all this session. I intend to support the Budget because I believe that its proposals are in the right direction. When it was decided to
5 p.m. make changes, I was naturally anxious that these changes should

be, as far as possible, in the interests of both consumers and producers, and that has been accomplished. It is not necessary for me to go into details. There is no doubt about that. I have discovered it, and discovered it in no uncertain way.

Now, I believe that in the interests of the whole of Canada, in the interests of unity, and national development, it is absolutely necessary that whatever Government may happen to be in power in the course of the next year, or itwo or three years, should take hold of this question and endeavour to solve it in some way or other.
